title: Hyderabad Man Dies in US 17 Days After Wedding; Family Seeks Jaishankar's Help
excerpt: Mohammed Jaber Hussain, 27, died in Lowell, Massachusetts, on September 14. His family, citing financial hardship, has appealed to EAM S. Jaishankar and Hyderabad MP Asaduddin Owaisi for help bringing his body home.
body:
• Mohammed Jaber Hussain, 27, of Santoshnagar, Hyderabad, died in Lowell, Massachusetts, on September 14 — 17 days after his August 28 wedding in Texas.
  • The cause of death has not been officially established; the family is awaiting postmortem and medical reports. He had spoken to his mother at around 8 am that morning and appeared fine.
  • MBT spokesperson Amjed Ullah Khan has appealed to External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar to get the Indian mission in the US to coordinate the repatriation; Hyderabad MP Asaduddin Owaisi has also sought the Centre's help.
  • The family says it belongs to an economically weaker section and is seeking government assistance to cover the steep cost of bringing Hussain's body home for final rites.

Death in Lowell

Mohammed Jaber Hussain, a 27-year-old engineer from Hyderabad's Santoshnagar, died in Lowell, Massachusetts, on Monday, September 14 — barely two and a half weeks after getting married in Texas. His family is now pleading with the central government to help bring his remains back to India for final rites.

According to media reports, Hussain spoke to his mother at around 8 am on September 14 and appeared fine. Hours later, the family received word that he had died while sleeping. The cause of death has not been officially established, and the family is awaiting postmortem and medical reports before anything can be confirmed, according to Y This News.

A young engineer, weeks into marriage

Hussain moved to the United States in 2021 to pursue a master's degree in civil engineering. He completed the degree at the University of New Haven in Connecticut in 2023 and subsequently worked for several engineering firms, according to Y This News. He had married in Texas on August 28 and later returned to Massachusetts, where he was living and working, while his wife remained in Texas. The couple had been preparing to begin their married life together, the reports said.

Faced with unfamiliar paperwork and the steep cost of repatriation, Hussain's parents approached Majlis Bachao Tehreek (MBT) spokesperson Amjed Ullah Khan for assistance. Khan has appealed to External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar to intervene and ask the Indian Embassy in Washington or the Consulate General of India in New York to coordinate with American authorities on the repatriation, according to 7Globe.

Hyderabad MP Asaduddin Owaisi has also sought the Centre's assistance for the family, including help with travel arrangements for Hussain's relatives, according to reports.

How repatriation from the US works

For grieving families, bringing a body home from the United States is a slow, expensive process. When the death is sudden or unexplained, a medical examiner's investigation must conclude before the remains are released. The Indian mission then issues a No Objection Certificate, and the body must be embalmed — mandatory for international transport of human remains — and placed in a hermetically sealed casket before an airline will accept it.

The cost is the harder barrier. International repatriation from the US typically runs into several thousand dollars: embalming, a sealed casket, air freight, and funeral-home fees on both ends. That is why families in such tragedies routinely turn to elected representatives and the External Affairs Ministry — consular intervention can unlock fee waivers, expedited paperwork, and community funds. The family's statement that it belongs to an economically weaker section underscores why, without that help, the logistics alone could stall the return.

What happens next

The immediate next step is the postmortem report, which will determine the cause of death and unlock the release of the body. Khan has urged Indian authorities to press for swift coordination with US officials so the remains can be flown to Hyderabad for final rites. The family's financial appeal — for the repatriation itself and for relatives to travel — now rests with the government.
nri_angle: A Hyderabad family's sudden loss in Massachusetts exposes the financial and bureaucratic burden diaspora families face repatriating loved ones from the US, and their routine reliance on EAM intervention and consular coordination.
author: Diaspora Desk
